extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and educated general readers interested in architectural theory and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts prescriptive principles and evaluative standards for designing and judging architecture, as set out in Ruskin's The Seven Lamps of Architecture. Emphasizes moral, aesthetic, and material criteria for buildings (especially devotional and memorial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: “Architecture is the art which so disposes and adorns the edifices raised by man for whatsoever uses, that the sight of them contributes to his mental health, power and pleasure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture's primary purpose is aesthetic and moral: arranging and adorning buildings so that their appearance benefits observers' mental health, power, and pleasure. This ties architectural success to the effect of sight on human well-being rather than mere utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Architecture from Building
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture concerns only those characters of an edifice “which are above and beyond its common use.” Building (e.g., church-building, ship-building) is the practical art of making something stand or perform a function; architecture is the addition of unnecessary-but-meaningful adornment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether features are purely functional (building) or ornamental/expressive (architecture). Examples of non-architectural functional features include the height of a breastwork or position of a bastion; examples of architectural features include a cable-moulding added without structural necessity or carved rounded courses beneath projecting masses. Anti-pattern: treating engineering/utility as equivalent to architectural quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Architectural Purposes (Five Heads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture naturally arranges itself under five heads: Devotional, Memorial, Civil, Military, Domestic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to assess which principles are most applicable: some lamps/principles have fuller reference to certain kinds of building (e.g., the Lamp of Sacrifice is especially relevant to devotional and memorial architecture). When judging or designing, attend to the building's class to weight applicable virtues appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lamp of Sacrifice (offer best and costly materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of Sacrifice prompts the offering of precious things merely because they are precious; of two marbles equally suitable one would choose the more costly; of two decorations equally effective one would choose the more elaborate so as to present more cost and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two forms: (a) private self-denial practiced for discipline, and (b) public offering to honor another (the latter usually most appropriate for architecture). In practice apply by choosing superior materials, more elaborate workmanship, and visible cost as an offering. Anti-pattern: modern tendency to maximize results at minimal cost. Moral/biblical justification provided: offerings to God should be the best of their kind; costliness often marks acceptableness (Ruskin cites Levitical examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offerings must be the best of their kind
rubrics_metrics.description: In offerings (and by analogy in architectural ornament and materials) the condition of acceptableness is that they should be the best of their kind—‘the best of the flock.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether selected materials/workmanship represent the best available within their kind; rejecting cheaper, inferior substitutes is a criterion of respect and honor. The text argues that offering inferior materials indicates a grudging or dishonoring feeling and thus is unacceptable for sacred/memorial works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of Purpose: 'Know what you have to do, and do it.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Success depends less on means or labor than on a clear understanding of the thing actually to be done. Confusion of means with ends causes failure; inquiry into capabilities must not precede the determination of what is desirable and right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before deciding methods or materials, define the desired moral/aesthetic purpose of the work. Avoid letting practical calculations preempt or limit the conception of the good design. Practical implication: design decisions should start from a clearly articulated aim and then select means to serve that aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek general, constant laws of right (principles over particulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than policing innumerable particular abuses, the art should seek some constant, general, and irrefragable laws of right—laws based on man's nature rather than on historical practice alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or creating architecture, prefer principles that are broadly applicable across styles and times (e.g., relation to human dignity, moral purpose) rather than ephemeral rules tied to momentary fashions. Use these laws as guides when novel materials or functions arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite the technical and imaginative; resist materialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture unites technical and imaginative elements as essentially as humanity does soul and body; there is a liability for the constructive (material/technical) element to prevail over the reflective (creative/aesthetic) element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether technical requirements dominate to the detriment of imaginative expression or whether a balance is achieved. Designs should preserve the purity and simplicity of the reflective element while satisfying structural needs. Anti-pattern: allowing engineering convenience to suppress aesthetic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and devotional dimension: architecture as an offering and expression of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural acts have dignity both in manner and motive; even small actions (drawing a line, a syllable) can be done truly and ennobled by motive. Architecture may honor God and reflect moral virtues like truth, decision, and temperance; its acceptableness can be judged by relation to moral/religious ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess designs not only by visual effect but by the moral quality of intention and the extent to which they embody virtues. For devotional/memorial architecture, consider whether the work expresses reverence through sacrifice of the best materials, labor, and thought. Anticipate objections about mixing sacred language: Ruskin defends referring to religious principles as a test of right action in artistic endeavors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ornamentation as meaningful offering (ornament must serve expressive/ceremonial ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamentation is architectural when it adds characters unnecessary to common use but venerable or beautiful; ornament as offering should be chosen because it is precious or expressive, not merely functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ornament by whether it meaningfully expresses value or devotion rather than being gratuitous or purely cost-saving decoration. Examples: carved mouldings or trefoiled heads that serve no defensive or functional need become architecture when they convey thought/price and honor. Anti-pattern: ornament used only to mask poor construction or to cheaply simulate value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principled use of historical precedent and selective exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin presents principles illustrated by one or two carefully chosen examples (Italian Romanesque, Gothic, Venetian, Norman) and warns against attempting exhaustive historical survey; principles should be inferred from exemplary buildings rather than slavishly copied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying standards, prefer deep study of exemplary cases to mere accumulation of precedents. Use examples to illuminate principles, not as fixed templates to be reproduced without understanding. Anti-pattern: treating many particulars of past practice as immutable rules.
